text:
Montana conducted surveys in the upper Armell's Creek and Colstrip area in 1970 and 1973. Five sites were located and assigned identification numbers. In 1972 the university also conducted a survey along the right-of-way of the Burlington Northern Railroad Sarpy Creek spur and located eighteen sites. In these surveys the type of sites, the pattern of distribution, and the artifacts recovered were similar to those found in the Westmoreland Resources lease area.
It may be surmised from the archaeological data that Sarpy Creek Valley was used in prehistoric times as a summer hunting and food gathering grounds as well as a passage way from the Yellowstone valley to the upper reaches of Tongue River, Rosebud Creek, and the Little Big Horn. There were no significant bison jumps, elaborate ceremonial structures, extensive occupation sites, unusual structures, etc. found. Appendix G should be consulted for a more detailed description of archaeological sites.
Early Crow History
The Absaroka or Crow were the first of the modern Plains Tribes to have migrated into this part of the northern plains, arriving about 1700-1725. The Suhtai, predecessor tribe of the modern Cheyenne, was also reported to have used the area for summer hunting and food gathering; but this tribe came into the region after the Crow Tribe did.

Neither tribe claimed substantial attachment to the Sarpy Creek area, as they found other places, particularly along large rivers and mountain foot-hills, more hospitable and suited to their way of life.
